meta.note: Story is DATA. v2 = two roads (hero/pawn) set at Post 3 that share physical posts but not scenes. DRAFT PROSE for all new scenes (Post 2 gate, all of Pawn's Road, pond routes/endings) — written to be revised by the owner. Hero's Road adapts the trail-tested v1 prose. Render order per scene: text -> choice result -> seasonalIntro(season) -> textCont -> variant(variants) -> endingVariant(endingVariants, only after choices settle) -> textAfter. A waypoint may hold `scenes` (picked by `when`, e.g. equals road) each carrying its OWN text/prompt/choices/wayfinding/next. A scene, a chosen choice, or a picked endingVariant may carry `ending` {tone, note, exits[]}; an exit may `commit` (dismiss a soft bad ending and walk on), `next` (bounce to a waypoint), or `reveal` terminal text.

crown.title: The Crown of the Mushroom King
crown.blurb: A shadowed wood, for the brave.

wp1.title: The Entrance
wp1.text:
A moth settles on the post beside you, its light guttering like a candle in a draft. “Traveler. Come close — closer, while my light still holds.” With every word the glow fades a little more. “I am the last of King Bolete’s messengers. The others, Lord Raggeth caught and snuffed out, one by one. I have flown a long way to find you, and I have not much left to burn.”

Behind it, the wood is wrong — grey, too silent, the smell of rot on the cold air.

“The king is dying. His crown is a ring of golden mushroom-caps — for what else would a mushroom-king wear? — and Lord Raggeth crept into the castle and tore three of those caps away. Where the crown goes dark, the forest follows. You can feel it already — the cold, the silence, the rot creeping root to root. By the last bell of nightfall the king’s heart will stop, and this wood will be Raggeth’s to rule: a kingdom of ash and bone. Three caps, scattered through the dark. Find them. Mend the crown. It is the only way left.”

It presses something small into your hand. “A honey-cake. There is little kindness left in this wood, traveler — spend yours well. It may cost more than you think. Go now. And trust no light but mine.”

wp2.title: Into the Forest
wp2.text:
You step off the road and the wood closes behind you like a held breath. The trees here are sick — bark gone black and weeping, leaves curled to ash. A small bird lies still in the path; the moth’s light passes over it and moves on, and does not look.

And the trees have faces — had you not noticed? Look again, as you walk. In the bark of the old ones: faces. Eyes and mouths and furrowed brows, watching you pass. “The forest’s old sentinels,” the moth says softly. “Awake since the first acorn fell. Once they sang to every traveler who came this way. But the king is dying, and one by one they have gone silent and still, their eyes drifting shut. They watch you now without a sound.”

The moth gathers what light it has, and tells you plainly what waits ahead, so you cannot say you were not warned:

“There are lights in this wood that wear a kind voice and a kind face, and they lead only to the bone-fields. There is a rot that spreads by touch and never, ever stops — it is the king’s dying, made into a thing that crawls. There are dead who do not rest, who guard to the grave what they died for. And there is Raggeth himself — who does not always kill what he catches. Sometimes he keeps it. Sometimes he turns it, and sends it back wearing your own face.”

Far off, a bell tolls — slow, and then slower. “The king’s heart,” the moth murmurs. “Hear how it fails. Three caps: one lies where a dying friend keeps watch, one where a false light feeds, one among the dead who were never avenged. This is the road ahead, traveler. It does not get kinder than here.”
wp2.prompt: Commit to the road ahead, or turn back?

choices.label: Go on into the dark
choices.text: You set your jaw and follow the leaning, half-rotted signpost deeper in. The moth’s light steadies, just a little, as if glad of company.

choices.label: Turn back — this is not my fight
choices.text: You turn for the road, and the daylight, and home. The moth does not plead. It only dims. Behind you, as you go, the last of its light gutters out, and the wood draws its silence closed over the king, and over the fox who waited, and over the dead who were never avenged. By morning there is no forest here at all — only ash, and bone, and a cold that came to stay. You were the last one it sent for.

wp3.title: The Great Old Tree
wp3.text:
Beneath the oldest tree, in the last patch the rot has not yet reached, a fox with one silver eye lies in the leaves. He is little more than bone and grey fur, and his breath comes shallow. He has guarded this place since before the tree stood tall — and now he is starving, for the blight has killed everything he might have hunted.

“I cannot move,” he says, and his voice is a thread. “I have not eaten in a week. I will not last the night.” Your hand finds the honey-cake. It is the only food you carry, and the night is long. This is the choice that sets your road.
wp3.prompt: Give him the honey-cake, or keep it?

choices.label: Give the honey-cake
choices.text: He eats slowly, gratefully, and when he is done his silver eye kindles like a struck coin. Strength returns to him by degrees. “Kindness,” he says softly, “is the first gold — rarer in this wood than any crown. You spent it on a dying old fox when you might have kept it for yourself.” From the moss he lifts a small golden cap and lays it in your palm. “I will not forget. When the dark is deepest, and every other light has failed you — look for my eye.” He rises, unsteady but alive, and slips into the shadows ahead, going before you. You will not walk this wood alone. This is the Hero’s Road.

choices.label: Keep it for yourself
choices.text:
You close your hand around the honey-cake and step around him. The fox says nothing — only watches you pass with his one silver eye, and you feel that eye on your back long after the trees have hidden him. There, in the leaves where he lies, the first golden cap gleams; it was the king’s, and the fox had no strength left to guard it. You lift it. Behind you, the old fox lowers his head to the cold ground. He will not see the morning.

And something in the wood feels the cruelty of it — a small coldness, given freely, in a place starved of warmth. Far off, in the deep of the trees, something that had been sleeping opens its eyes and turns, slow and pleased, toward you. You have opened a door. This is the Pawn’s Road.

wp4.title: The Fork
wp4.wayfinding: Take the path to your RIGHT. Do not continue straight.

scenes.text:
The path forks at a leaning post. The plain way bends off to your right — but straight ahead, where the trail runs on into the trees, a light is waiting. It is beautiful: a soft blue glow drifting in the dark, its voice cool and sweet as well-water. “Straight on, traveler — don’t turn aside. The straight way is the short way, the kind way. You’re so tired; let me lead you home.”

But the moth on your shoulder has gone rigid, its light pressed small. “That is the corpse-light,” it breathes. “Raggeth’s lure. It wants you to walk straight on. Look at the ground ahead — look.”

And you see them now, half-sunk in the moss along the path that runs straight on: bones. The picked-clean bones of travelers who kept walking toward the lovely light before you — tired, and trusting, and clever enough, they thought. The right-hand path holds no such light. It only holds the way through.
scenes.prompt: Walk straight toward the light, or see through it and turn right?

choices.label: See through it — turn right
choices.text: You turn your back on the light and take the plain right-hand path. Behind you the wisp’s sweetness curdles — to a shriek, to a hiss, to nothing — Raggeth’s lure, starved of you. There at the fork, just along the right-hand way, the second golden cap gleams in the moss. You lift it gently. “Cleverness is the second gold,” the moth says quietly. “Those others were not foolish — only trusting. They walked straight on. You did not. Remember that.”

choices.label: Walk straight toward the light
choices.text: You step toward it — and the instant you pass the fork, the light gutters out and the cold rushes in, and the bone-field opens at your feet, white and endless and waiting for one more. You are at the very edge of it when a weight hits your side and drags you back: the fox, silver eye blazing, jaws fixed in your sleeve, hauling you off the bones and onto the right-hand path. He does not let go until you are well clear. You have seen, up close, exactly how this wood ends a traveler — and you will not forget it; it leaves you harder than it found you. The second golden cap lies in the moss at the fork. You take it, and you owe the fox a debt you mean to pay. “Cleverness is dear-bought,” the moth says, shaken. “Now — go right. Always right.”

scenes.text:
The path forks at a leaning post, and the blue light is already waiting — but it does not flee from you, and it does not lure. It drifts close, and it speaks your name, softly, as though it has known you a long time.

“There you are. I have been watching you since the fox. You let him die — no, no, don’t flinch from it; it was honest. Why should you starve for a dying king and his dying wood? They sent you to spend yourself for them, child, the way they spent all the others whose bones lie just there.” The light warms, kind as a hearth. “I am Raggeth. Take my mark, and the rot will never touch you. Walk my wood untouched, while it lasts — and it will not last. The crown is going out. Be on the winning side of the dark.”

The moth on your shoulder has gone very still, and very afraid.
scenes.prompt: Refuse the mark, or accept it?

choices.label: Refuse the mark
choices.text: “No,” you say, before you can talk yourself out of it. The warmth goes out of the light all at once. “A pity,” says Raggeth, not unkindly. “Then you walk hunted. No fox. No friends. Only me, behind every tree, until the wood is mine.” The light withdraws, and you are alone in a way you have never been alone. There at the fork the second golden cap gleams; you take it with a steady hand. You are unmarked, unbroken — and entirely on your own. “Cleverness,” the moth whispers, the only voice left to you, “and the harder courage of being alone. Now — right. Always right.”

choices.label: Accept the mark
choices.text: You hold out your hand. Raggeth lays a cap in it — not gold, but a cold black thing, slick as a drowned mushroom, and it does not warm to your skin; your skin cools to it. On your shoulder the moth recoils, its light shrinking from you as from a flame turned wrong. And the wood — the wood looks different now. The dead in their cold ground look like enemies. The dying king looks like a fool who would not let go. The rot looks almost beautiful. “Good,” Raggeth breathes. “Walk on, my own. Go right — there is nothing on the straight road for you now but bones, and you are past needing those.” The second golden cap lies in the moss; you pocket it without quite knowing why you still want it.

scenes.text:
The trees give way to a small graveyard — a dozen old stones, leaning every which way in the grey light. These are the king’s knights, the last of the old mushroom-guard, who stood against Raggeth an age ago and fell to the last, and were never avenged. The wood forgot them. The rot has not — it creeps among the stones like spilled ink.

At the center stands one great cracked stone, and at its foot a candle, long gone cold. “The last cap is here,” the moth breathes, “in the keeping of the dead. They will not give it to the timid. You must wake their captain — and you must not look away when he wakes.”
scenes.prompt: Light the candle and wake the guardian, or tiptoe past?

choices.label: Light the candle
choices.text: Your hands shake so badly you can barely breathe on the wick — but it catches, one small gold flame in a sea of grey. The great stone splits. Something rises from it: a knight of blackened oak and toadstool, vast, its eyes two coals, an age of grief in its ruined face. It would be so easy to run. You do not run. For a long, cold moment the dead captain weighs you — then slowly bows. “Courage,” it says, in a voice like a closing tomb, “is the last gold, and it is bought with fear, not the lack of it.” It lays the third cap in your hand, and then it does not sink back. It takes up its broken sword and falls in at your shoulder. “We could not save the king. We will see you to him. And when you face Raggeth — for you will — we will not look away, and neither will you.” You walk on with a dead knight at your side.

choices.label: Tiptoe quietly past
choices.text: You cannot do it. You hold your breath and slip between the graves, quiet as the dead themselves, and you do not light the candle, and you do not wake the captain. The last cap you find at the graveyard’s edge, set upon a small stone — a young knight’s grave, one who fell too soon. You lift it with hands that will not stop shaking, and all across that little ground you feel the weight of eyes that hoped for more from you, and let you pass anyway. No knight rises to walk with you. But the fox is still ahead, and the moth is still at your shoulder, and that will have to be enough.

scenes.text:
The graveyard of the old mushroom-guard — the dead who fell resisting Raggeth, an age ago, and were never avenged. You feel them notice you the moment you step in. Not the cap on the stones: the cap in your pocket, the cold black one, and the chill of it spreading up your arm. The rot does not touch you now. The dead see exactly why.

The great cracked stone splits without a candle. The captain rises, two coals for eyes, and looks at the mark on you with something worse than anger — recognition. “We died to keep this from spreading,” it says, “and here it walks in wearing a child’s face.” It lifts the cold dead candle from the stone and holds it out to you. “This is the cure, and it is cruel. Light it, and it will burn the dark out of you — it will hurt like a little dying. Or keep your master’s gift, and go to the pond to take the crown for him, and we will not stop you, because you are already lost.”
scenes.prompt: Light the candle and burn the mark away, or refuse it?

choices.label: Light it — burn the mark away
choices.text: You touch the flame to the wick, and the cold black cap in your pocket catches like dry leaves, and it burns — through your hand, up your arm, into the place where Raggeth had begun to make a home. It is a little death. You go down on the cold ground and you come back up scarred, and shaking, and yourself again. The Cap of Courage is in your hand; you do not remember the captain placing it there. “Courage,” it says, quieter now, “is bought with fear — and sometimes with worse. You nearly became what we died fighting. You turned back from it. Few do.” The mark is gone. The scar will not be.

choices.label: Refuse it — turn on the dead
choices.text: You close your hand over your pocket, over the cold cap, and you back away from the candle and its cruel little fire. “Then take your courage and your curse together,” the captain says, and there is no anger left in it, only a vast tiredness. The third cap it sets on the nearest stone; you take it, because some part of you still counts to three. The dead sink down and do not watch you go. The mark has the whole of you now. The wood ahead looks like spoils. You climb toward the pond to take the crown — and you know, without being told, who you mean to give it to.

scenes.text:
The graveyard of the old mushroom-guard — the dead who stood against Raggeth and fell, and were never avenged. You come among them alone, hunted, unmarked, the corpse-light’s refusal still cold in your chest.

The great cracked stone splits without a candle, and the captain rises, two coals for eyes — and looks at you a long moment, and slowly bows. “We know what you turned down at the fork,” it says, in a voice like a closing tomb. “He offered you the easy road and you spat on it, and you have walked alone ever since. That is its own courage — the cold kind, the kind with no one watching.” It lays the third cap in your hand. “We cannot walk with you; we are bound to this ground. But you have earned this clean. Go to the pond unbroken. Few reach it so.” The dead sink back. You are still alone — but you carry all three caps, and you carry them as your own.

wp6.title: The Way to the Pond
wp6.text:
Three caps, cold in your hand, and the wood gone nearly black around you. The moth’s light is a dying ember now; it can barely lift from your shoulder. The bell — the king’s heart — tolls once more, so faint you feel it more than hear it, and the silence that follows runs on too long before the next.

“Hurry,” the moth breathes. “He is almost gone. The path climbs from here — the pond lies above us, at the top of the wood, where the forest was born, and where, tonight, it may die.” The signpost points the way up into the dark. You climb.

wp7.title: The Pond
wp7.text: The climb brings you out at the pond — the old heart-well of the forest, whose waters rise and fall with the king’s own life.

seasonalIntro.text: The water lies black and brimming and still — yet no stars float in it, for the sky itself has gone dark. “The last of the king’s strength,” the moth murmurs, “pooled here, and waiting, while it holds.”

Where deep water should be there is only a cracked and shrinking hollow, a last puddle sinking into mud. “The pond drains as the king does,” the moth breathes. “Nearly empty now. We are nearly too late.”

scenes.textCont: On a toadstool throne at the water’s edge sits King Bolete — or what remains of him: grey to the bone, cracked like old wood, the mushrooms of his crown wilted brown. “You came,” he says, no louder than a breath. “And you did not come alone — I feel them with you.” You kneel at the throne, and one for a kindness, one for a cleverness, one for a courage, you press the three golden caps home into the bare ring of the crown. Light wakes in it. The king’s eyes open. “It is done — and now the wood asks one more thing of you. Which way will you carry what you’ve mended?”
scenes.prompt: Choose your way from the pond.

choices.label: Take the long loop, and let the wood heal as you walk
Go on into the deep wood, to face Raggeth for good

endingVariants.text: You go down into the deep wood with the crown blazing and your friends at your side — the silver-eyed fox before you, the dead knight at your shoulder, the moth burning whole and bright again. Raggeth meets you in the last dark, and he is terrible, and you do not look away — none of you do — and between the four of you the dark one is broken at last, an age of grief paid back in a single night. The light pours out of the crown and out through the whole black wood, and the dying simply stops, and then reverses: green running up the black trunks, the face-trees waking and beginning, very quietly, to sing. “You did not walk my wood alone,” the king says, “because you would not let others walk theirs alone. Come — there is a castle, and a treasure in it, and the night is young after all.”

You go down into the deep wood to end it, though you are not all you might have been — a clever heart but no knight at your back, or a brave one but a step too slow at the fork. Raggeth is broken; the wood is saved; but the dark does not go quietly, and it takes someone dear as it falls. The moth burns out to light your last step — or the fox throws himself between you and the end of it and does not rise. You carry the crown home mended and the forest living, and you carry a grief in it that will not lift. “You won,” the king says softly. “Not everyone who won tonight will see the dawn. Remember the one who bought it for you.”

You take the long way down, the loop through the lower wood, in no hurry now that the crown is lit — and that is its own kind of mending. Everywhere your slow feet pass, the rot draws back a little further into the earth; the longer walk gives the forest time to truly begin. By the time you reach the meadow at the bottom of the wood, green and gold and loud with the first bees, the dark has lost its grip root to root. “The fast cure and the slow cure both heal,” the king says, “but the slow one heals deeper. You gave the wood your time. It will not forget that either.”

You take the short way home, and the king lives, and the wood will live — but you flinched, once, in the graveyard, when it counted, and no knight walks you out. The fox sees you to the tree-line and the moth lights you to the road, and they are kind, and it is quieter than it might have been. You saved him. You will always know you might have given a little more. “A good ending,” the king says, “and a lonelier one than you deserved. Be braver next time, child. There is always a next time, in a wood.”

You take the short way home, the crown mended and the king’s heart steadying behind you, and your friends walk you out: the fox at your heel, the knight at your shoulder if he rose for you, the moth bright overhead. The wood opens at last into a wide and sunlit meadow, green and gold and thick with flowers — the whole bright opposite of the dark you walked. The king will live to see the dawn, and maybe many dawns; the dark may yet come again, but not tonight, and not for you. “Rest here a while,” the king says. “You have earned the light.”

The crown is mended and the king will live. Your friends walk you out of the dark and into a wide, sunlit meadow at the foot of the wood, green and gold and loud with bees. The dark may come again, but not tonight. “Rest here a while,” the king says. “You have earned the light.”

scenes.textCont: On a toadstool throne at the water’s edge sits King Bolete — grey to the bone, cracked like old wood, his crown a bare dark ring. “You came,” he breathes, and then he sees the cold thing in you, and his failing eyes close. “Ah. So that is how it is.” You carry his three caps. You do not kneel to mend them. The mark in you knows another use for a crown.
scenes.prompt: Where do you carry the crown?

choices.label: Into the deep wood — to Raggeth
Out of the wood, the way you came

exits.label: Accept the dark — THE END
exits.reveal: You carry the crown down into the deep wood and set the caps yourself into the cold ring, and they wake the wrong way — a black light, a crown for the dark one. Raggeth takes it from your hands almost tenderly. “My herald,” he says. You turn, and the wood goes out behind you, root to root, the face-trees’ eyes closing one last time. The king’s heart stops between one silence and the next. You walk at the dark one’s side now, wearing your own face, and you do not remember why that should trouble you.

exits.label: The wood grants one last mercy — flee
exits.reveal: Something stops your hand on the cold ring — the memory of a silver eye, maybe, or the moth’s small light guttering one final time at the very edge of you. You drop the crown and you run. The trees, dying, part for you anyway — one last kindness from a wood you betrayed — and spit you out into grey daylight at the road’s edge, shaking, empty-handed, alive. Behind you the forest falls dark. But your feet are on the road, and they are still yours, and they carry you home.

endingVariants.text: [DRAFT — Pawn’s Road, fallen. You bear the king’s caps down into the deep wood, toward the one whose mark you wear.]

exits.label: Accept the dark — THE END
exits.reveal: You bear the crown out of the wood the way you came in — but it is no rescue you carry it to. Raggeth is waiting at the tree-line as though he always was, and you set the golden caps into the cold ring and crown him with your own two hands, there in the last of the daylight. The forest dies behind you both, quietly, completely. He keeps you. You wear your own face still, which is the cruelest part, and you have quite forgotten there was ever anything wrong with that.

exits.label: The wood grants one last mercy — flee
exits.reveal: At the very tree-line, with the cold ring in your hands, you stop. You think of the fox you let die, and for the first time it is unbearable. You let the crown fall in the leaves and you run — out of the wood, into the grey ordinary light of the road, empty-handed and shaking and free. The forest goes dark behind you. You could not save it. You saved the last small part of yourself, and some nights that will have to be enough.

endingVariants.text: [DRAFT — Pawn’s Road, fallen. You carry the king’s caps back out of the wood — but not to safety.]

scenes.textCont: On a toadstool throne at the water’s edge sits King Bolete — grey to the bone, cracked like old wood, the mushrooms of his crown wilted brown. “You came,” he breathes. “And you came back to yourself along the way; I can see the scar of it. That is harder than never falling.” You kneel at the throne, and you set the three golden caps home into the bare ring of the crown. Light wakes in it — thinner than the bright roads, but true. “Now choose,” the king says. “Which way will you carry what you’ve mended?”
scenes.prompt: Choose your way from the pond.

choices.label: Out of the wood, the short way home
On into the deep wood, to face Raggeth

endingVariants.text: You mend the crown alone, as you did everything else since the fork — no fox, no knight, no mark, only your own two unbroken hands. The king lives; the wood will live; and no friends come from the shadows to thank you, because you made none, and you asked for none. You walk out into a cold and lonely dusk, unbroken, unbowed, unthanked. “You never sold yourself,” the king says quietly, “though I think he offered you the world. Some walkers I remember for their friends. You, I will remember for your spine.”

You go down into the deep wood with the mended crown and the burn of the cure still raw in you, and you face Raggeth wearing the scar where his mark used to be. He knows you. “You were nearly mine,” he says, almost wounded. “I was,” you answer, “and I came back.” That is the thing he cannot abide, and it is the thing that breaks him. The wood is saved. You carry the scar of what you almost became out of the dark with you, and you will carry it always. “You mended more than a crown tonight,” the king says. “Be gentle with the place it healed.”

You take the short way out, the mended crown behind you and the king’s heart beating again, and you walk home hollowed out by how close it was — how near you came to carrying that same crown to the dark one instead. The wood will live. You saved it, barely, and the barely is what stays with you. “You came back from the edge of yourself,” the king says, “and that is no small mending. Go easy. The hollow fills again, in time, if you let it.”
